title: Mae and Rook's River Lights
markdown:
Mae was a field mouse, small and sprightly, with whiskers that wiggled at every curious thought. She usually hid when things got tricky, preferring the safety of her cozy burrow under the old apple tree. Her paws were quick. Her heart was warm as a sunbeam. Her courage was usually tucked away for a rainy day.

Rook was a castle jackdaw, feathers as dark as midnight, a voice that cawed with booming bravado. He was quite clever, always observing from the battlements. Sometimes he was a little too proud to admit he did not have all the answers. He meant well.

In a land of sleepy villages and a bustling castle, a peculiar thing began to happen with the river ferry. The Whispering River flowed as merrily as a giggling brook, right past the town square. Usually the ferry, a sturdy old barge steered by a kind round man named Silas, would dock on one side, paddle across, and come back again. Regular as sunrise.

Then the ferry started to get confused. A little nudge. A little swerve. As if the river were playing tag with Silas’s long steering pole. The barge bumped with a hollow thump against the wrong bank.

“Oh dear,” Silas would sigh, brow furrowed. “Not again.”

The villagers relied on him to get to market, to visit friends, to fetch supplies. They needed fresh bread and juicy apples. But the ferry kept docking on the wrong side. It ferried folk to the sweet-smelling meadow when they wanted the noisy baker. It brought them to the shade of the old wise oak when they urgently needed the clanging blacksmith. Topsy-turvy.

Mae peeked from her tiny door. Whiskers quivered. “Why can’t the ferry just go to the right place?” she whispered, paws tucked neatly beneath her, a habit when she felt shy. Loud noises made her jump. Big open spaces made her feel like a speck of dust in a hurricane.

Rook, high on the battlements, saw everything with sharp bright eyes. He cawed down, a bold booming sound.

“Silas. You’ve missed it again. The baker is on the other side, you old feather-brain.”

Silas shook his head, round face etched with frustration and bewilderment. “It’s no use, Rook. The river, or perhaps the ferry itself, seems to have a mind of its own. Like hide-and-seek.”

The problem lasted three whole days. Bread late for breakfast. The blacksmith’s hammer with fewer cheerful bongs. Villagers’ smiles wilting. On the fourth day the whole village was in a huff, a low grumbling hum like bees.

That evening the sun painted the sky orange and rosy pink. Mae scurried home along the dusty path with a tickle of worry in her chest. The ferry problem was making everyone unhappy, and Mae did not like unhappiness. She wanted to help. How could a tiny mouse help a big confused ferry? She felt so very small.

A familiar sharp caw. Rook swooped down onto a low sturdy branch of her apple tree, right above the burrow.

“Mae. Still fretting about that wobbly boat, eh?”

Her whiskers drooped. “It’s just so topsy-turvy, Rook. And everyone is cross. It makes the air feel prickly.”

Rook puffed his chest. “Wobbly, yes. Confused, certainly. But I’ve been watching. Silas tries his very best, bless his round heart, but the current, or something unseen, keeps pulling him off course. Like trying to hit a moving target in the dark.”

“In the dark?” Mae squeaked.

“Not quite dark,” Rook amended, tapping his beak. “But you know how the castle guards sometimes light those big fire baskets on poles? To send signals to the watchtowers on the hills? They pass messages very quickly that way, even when it’s getting dim.”

Mae blinked. Fire baskets on poles. Sending signals. Very quickly. She thought of Silas struggling with his pole, of disappointed sighs. Silas needed to know which bank was the right bank, right now, before he got too far off course.

“Rook,” she said, voice trembling a little, a new spark in it. “What if we used fire baskets? Not for the castle. For the ferry.”

Rook cocked his head, black eyes gleaming. “Fire baskets? For a ferry? How, little Mae? It sounds like a rather large undertaking for a small mouse.”

“The ferry always needs to go to the same places. To the baker’s side, where the bread smells so good. To the market side, where the colourful stalls are. What if, when the ferry is supposed to go to the baker’s, we light a fire basket on that bank? A bright clear flame. And when it’s supposed to go to the market, we light one on that bank.”

Rook hopped from foot to foot. “Aha. A beacon. A river beacon. So Silas knows precisely where to aim. Brilliant, Mae. Absolutely brilliant.”

A plan formed as surely as a cloud. Mae, despite her fear of open fields and being seen, knew where the best driest kindling lived. Rook, with strong wings, could carry the larger twigs and help spark the fires with clever beak-work.

Next morning, as soon as the first golden rays touched the town, they were busy. Scurrying and swooping. Fallen branches. Dry leaves. Fluffy moss. Mae’s usual fear of being seen felt smaller than her growing excitement. Rook carried bundles of twigs almost as big as himself.

They found two long sturdy poles leaning against the barn. They tied tight bundles of dry leaves and moss to the top of each with strong grass, perfect for catching a spark. Small fire baskets, really, just big enough to be seen from the river, like cheerful little lanterns.

“Now, remember,” Rook cawed, a little softer than usual. “The baker lives on the side with the big cheerful red roof. The market stalls are near the grumpy goose pond. The one where the geese always honk at everyone.”

Mae nodded, heart thumping like a tiny drum. “Baker’s side. Red roof. Market side. Grumpy goose pond.” She took a deep breath. A strange calm settled.

As Silas steered the ferry away from the morning mist, they scampered to their positions. Mae, feeling a thrill of bravery she had never known, lit the tinder on the pole near the baker’s house. A tiny flame flickered, then grew with a gentle crackle, a cheerful welcoming glow. Rook flew to the other bank and, with an expert nudge of his beak, lit the pole near the goose pond.

Silas squinted, scanning the banks. He saw the flames. Clear bright signals. He steered with a new certainty, hands steady on the pole. The current, which had seemed a mischievous trickster, now felt like a helpful hand.

“Hooray,” cried the villagers, as the ferry glided smoothly to the baker’s side, right where it was supposed to be.

Mae watched from her hiding spot, a shy happy smile on her tiny face. Rook swooped down beside her with a proud caw.

“We did it, Mae. We showed that river who’s boss.”

The ferry kept docking on the correct bank all day. The baker sold all his crusty bread. Even the grumpy geese seemed a little less grumpy. Mae did not announce that she had become the clever helper of the Whispering River. She only sat under the apple tree with Rook, watching Silas pole back toward the red roof as if the river had, at last, agreed to make up its mind.
